newsitem.title: USA: Controversy looms as U.S. report on CPI nears.
newsitem.headline: Controversy looms as U.S. report on CPI nears.

text.p: A congressionally appointed panel is preparing to unveil recommendations to improve the government's inflation gauge that could save billions of dollars from the federal budget in coming years.
But analysts are already predicting controversy.
For the past year and a half, the commission named by the Senate Finance Committee has been studying suspected flaws in the Labor Department's Consumer Price Index.

The five-member panel, which is led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin, on Wednesday plans to release its final report. The report is expected to conclude that the monthly CPI overstates inflation by a percentage point a year or more.
The report could figure prominently in the budget talks getting underway between the Republican-controlled Congress and the White House.
"This CPI report has the potential to be either a deal-maker or a deal-breaker," said Stan Collender, budget analyst at marketing and consulting firm Burson-Marsteller.

The CPI, which attempts to capture changes in what consumers pay for everything from a head of lettuce to a visit to the doctor, is used to index benefits for costly programs such as Social Security. It is also used to adjust income-tax brackets.
Even a relatively small downward adjustment to the CPI could effectively cut spending and boost revenues by a substantial amount, especially when the effects are added up over several years.
Still, Collender and other experts said it remains to be seen whether the suggestions will be implemented anytime soon.

"Don't hold your breath," cautioned Robert Reischauer, a former director of the Congressional Budget Office who is now a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank. "Politically, I don't see it happening, although that doesn't mean I don't think it would be a good thing."
A number of prominent economists, including Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, have backed the idea of adjusting the CPI.

However, critics, including the influential American Association of Retired Persons, have denounced many of the proposals as little more than a "back-door effort" to cut entitlement programs and raise taxes.
Many experts said the specifics of the Boskin commission's recommendations on the CPI could matter a great deal in determining the chances for success.
Economist Charles Lieberman of Chase Securities said the panel's recommendations would likely take one of three forms:
-- Congress could enact legislation to index entitlement programs to the CPI less the amount of the suspected bias
-- Congress could mandate creation of a new index
-- or the panel could suggest ways that the Labor Department could fix the existing index.

"The problem with the first two potential recommendations is that someone would have to take explicit responsibility for reducing Social Security benefits," Lieberman said, adding that both President Clinton and the Republican-led Congress would be reluctant to do that.
Collender agreed that sensitivity to politics might prevent solutions involving legislative changes. "If nobody wants to go first, the savings will just sit there," he said.

The less politically charged alternative of placing the burden on the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics also has drawbacks, Lieberman said. "It requires the bureau to agree with (the commission's) analysis," he said.
